headline: Holgate's South Bowl Cut Deepens — Bass Feeding the Trough After Dark
subhead: The bunker push we flagged last week finally hit Barnegat Light, while fluke keep grinding on the inlet edges through the heat.
body_markdown:
Flew the drone over the south bowl at Holgate before the sun was even up Sunday, and the cut's changed shape again. That inside trough that's been running parallel to the beach for the last three weeks has pushed another fifteen, twenty yards south and dug deeper — I'd guess four to five feet on the low now where it was barely three. The 3-foot swell out of the southeast that's been rolling through at a 7-second period isn't big, but it's steady enough to keep working that sandbar, and steady swell at low period like that reshapes structure faster than people think. That trough is holding bait right now — you can see the nervous water in the drone footage, peanut bunker and mullet stacked tight against the drop.

That's exactly where the bass are living, but only after the sun goes down. Daytime water on the ocean side is sitting in the mid-to-upper 70s — 75.7 out at the buoy off the Bight — and stripers in that kind of warm water go nocturnal and structure-bound. During the day they're deep on the Barnegat Light rocks and under the Ship Bottom and Beach Haven bridge pilings, not eating much of anything worth chasing. Come dusk they slide up onto the bars and into cuts like that Holgate trough to hunt. I fished it two nights this week on the last two hours of the outgoing, swimming a black Bomber Long A slow through the trough, and connected on three fish, biggest going 29 inches. Eels fished on a fishfinder rig tight to the Barnegat Light north jetty rocks after dark have been the more consistent producer for the guys putting in the hours — that's the play right now, and it's about to matter more. We're sliding into a neap tide the next couple days, currents softening up through the 5th and 6th, which means less water movement to trigger a bite. When that happens the bass compress into the strongest current windows and the deepest structure they can find — the Little Egg Inlet gut and the bridge pilings become the spots worth your night hours over the next week.

The bluefish news is the one I called last week and it's playing out almost exactly on schedule. Bunker pods pushing south out of the Belmar corridor have reached Barnegat Inlet and are starting to funnel past Beach Haven on the tide changes, and the blitzes are following them in. Guys working the outside of the Barnegat jetty on the last of the incoming this week found surface chaos — bunker getting bulldozed, blues in the 3 to 6 pound range crushing everything, best on wide swimming plugs and 2-ounce Kastmasters worked fast through the froth. It's not an all-day thing yet — the pods are still moving, not settled — but if they hold like they did in past years, Beach Haven Inlet and the water off Holgate's north end should get their turn within the next tide cycle or two.

Fluke are still the most dependable meal ticket on this stretch, and this is peak season for it. Doormat-class fish are showing on the ocean structure off Beach Haven — the reef pieces in 25 to 35 feet — and in the rip line right off Little Egg Inlet where the outgoing current dumps bay water into the ocean and stacks bait against the shoal edge. White Gulp Swimming Mullets on ¾-ounce bucktails, dragged slow on the drift through that rip, have been putting keepers in the box, with a few fish pushing 5 and 6 pounds mixed into a lot of shorts that need throwing back. Inside, the channel edges through Great Bay and up toward Graveling Point are producing too, though smaller — spearing and Gulp combos on light jig heads, working the deeper bends where the current sweeps bait off the flats on the outgoing.

Weakfish are a bonus right now, not a target — scattered fish showing in the Manahawkin channels and the deeper cuts of Barnegat Bay, mostly picked up by guys fluking who happen to hook one on a Gulp shrimp worked slow near bottom on the last hour of the tide. Nothing like the Delaware Bay run, but worth a cast or two if you're already back there. Kingfish are still working the ocean wash from Ship Bottom down through Holgate on bloodworm and Fishbites rigs fished tight to the beach on a slow incoming — small fish, good for a chowder, not much more. Black drum are basically done for the year up in the Mullica and Graveling Point flats — that spring window closed weeks ago and they've pushed back out to deeper water.

Looking ahead, the neap tide through midweek is going to soften everything up — less current means the bass window narrows to the peak of the tide swing and the deepest structure, so plan night trips around the strongest hour of movement rather than fishing the whole cycle. If the bunker keep pushing south the way they have been, I'd expect the blitz activity at Barnegat and Beach Haven inlets to build through the week rather than fade — that's the one to watch closely on the tide changes. Fluke should hold steady on the ocean structure as long as this water stays warm and stable, though the bite's been more grind-it-out than easy — expect to cull through a lot of shorts for your keepers right now.
